Article Title: A 13-year-old boy was airlifted after a rabid beaver attacked him at a Maryland state park, forcing officials to close the swimming beach
Article Text:
What happened at Cunningham Falls State Park?

Why did officials close the swimming beach?



The beaver later tested positive for rabies

Why are attacks by beavers so rare?



What is rabies and why is it so dangerous?



About Cunningham Falls State Park

A summer outing at one of Maryland's most popular state parks turned into a frightening medical emergency after a 13-year-old boy was attacked by a beaver while swimming. The incident occurred on Sunday morning at the William Houck Area of Cunningham Falls State Park in Frederick County, where the boy suffered bite injuries to his hands and chest. He was airlifted to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for treatment as authorities immediately closed the swimming beach and launched a search for the animal. Officials later confirmed that a captured beaver tested positive for rabies, raising concerns about public safety and prompting an ongoing investigation into the unusual wildlife attack.According to the Maryland Department of Natural Resources and local reports, the attack took place at around 9:10 a.m. on Sunday in the designated swimming area near North Beach at the William Houck Area of Cunningham Falls State Park. The teenager was swimming when a beaver suddenly attacked him, biting his hands and chest.Emergency responders arrived quickly, and due to the nature of the injuries and the potential risk of rabies exposure, the boy was flown by Maryland State Police helicopter to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for specialised medical care.Authorities have not released updates on his condition.Soon after the attack, officials closed the swimming beach to protect visitors while wildlife officers searched for the beaver responsible.Personnel from the Maryland Park Service, Maryland Natural Resources Police and wildlife officials searched the lake to locate the animal. The rest of Cunningham Falls State Park remained open, but access to the swimming area was restricted until officials could determine whether the threat had been removed.Authorities later captured one beaver and continued monitoring the area to ensure there were no additional risks to the public.Laboratory testing later confirmed that the captured beaver was infected with rabies, a viral disease that attacks the nervous system of mammals and is almost always fatal once symptoms develop.Officials are continuing to determine whether the captured animal was the same beaver involved in the attack. Because rabies can spread through bites and saliva, anyone exposed to a potentially rabid animal requires immediate medical evaluation. The teenager is expected to receive appropriate post-exposure treatment as part of his care.Although beavers are among North America's largest rodents, they are generally shy animals that avoid people. They spend most of their time building dams, lodges and gathering vegetation.Wildlife experts say beavers rarely attack humans unless they feel cornered, are protecting their young or are suffering from illnesses such as rabies. An unprovoked attack on a swimmer is therefore considered highly unusual and immediately raised concerns among wildlife officials.Rabid animals often display abnormal behaviour, including aggression, disorientation and a reduced fear of humans, making encounters significantly more dangerous than normal.Rabies is caused by a virus that affects the brain and spinal cord of mammals. It spreads primarily through bites from infected animals, although saliva entering an open wound or mucous membrane can also transmit the disease.Once clinical symptoms appear, rabies is almost always fatal. However, prompt treatment after exposure is highly effective. Medical care typically includes immediate wound cleaning, rabies immune globulin for unvaccinated individuals and a series of rabies vaccinations to prevent the virus from causing illness.Located in Maryland's scenic Catoctin Mountains, Cunningham Falls State Park is one of the state's most visited outdoor destinations. The William Houck Area features Hunting Creek Lake, a designated swimming beach, hiking trails, camping facilities, boating and picnic areas. The park is especially busy during the summer, attracting thousands of visitors looking to swim and enjoy outdoor recreation.The incident serves as a reminder that even well-managed recreational areas remain part of natural ecosystems where encounters with wildlife can occur.The Maryland Department of Natural Resources continues to investigate the attack while monitoring wildlife activity around the lake. Officials will determine when it is safe to reopen the swimming beach after ensuring that no further threat remains.In the meantime, visitors are encouraged to avoid approaching wild animals, report any wildlife displaying unusual behaviour and seek immediate medical attention if they are bitten or scratched by any mammal. Although rabid beavers are extremely rare, authorities say rapid reporting and treatment are essential to protecting public health.
Article Summary: 13-year-old boy airlifted to Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore for treatment. Authorities immediately closed the swimming beach and launched a search for the animal. Officials later confirmed that a captured beaver tested positive for rabies. Unprovoked attack on a swimmer is considered highly unusual.

Article Title: In 1934, this Pennsylvania mountain went from a hawk killing ground to the world's first raptor sanctuary and changed bird conservation forever
Article Text:
Why so many raptors pass over Hawk Mountain

When migration attracted hunters instead of birdwatchers

The birth of the world's first raptor sanctuary

The science behind Hawk Mountain's migration records

Which raptors can you see at Hawk Mountain

How to experience Hawk Mountain today

Every autumn, the skies above a forested ridge in eastern Pennsylvania fill with movement. Eagles drift on rising air, falcons streak across the horizon and kestrels appear in quick flashes before disappearing south. For generations, Hawk Mountain has been one of North America's best places to witness this seasonal migration because the landscape naturally funnels birds of prey along a narrow route through the Appalachian Mountains. Yet the ridge was not always known for conservation. Long before visitors arrived carrying binoculars and cameras, people climbed the same slopes with rifles.The transformation from a place where raptors were routinely shot to a protected sanctuary reshaped both bird conservation and the scientific study of migration, leaving a legacy that continues nearly a century later.Hawk Mountain sits within the Appalachian chain, where the shape of the landscape works in favour of migrating raptors. As birds travel between their breeding territories and wintering grounds, many avoid unnecessary effort by taking advantage of warm columns of rising air and favourable winds. The ridge creates ideal conditions for soaring flight, allowing large birds to cover long distances while using relatively little energy.That combination of geography and weather means thousands of raptors pass over the mountain during migration seasons. Some days bring only a steady trickle, while strong winds and good thermals can produce an almost continuous procession overhead. Visitors may watch bald eagles, broad-winged hawks, peregrine falcons and other species travelling within surprisingly close range.The conditions that concentrated birds also made Hawk Mountain attractive to hunters during the early twentieth century. Large numbers of raptors gathered in one place, creating easy targets as they crossed the ridge.At the time, birds of prey received little public sympathy. Hawks were widely viewed as pests because they hunted smaller birds and farm animals, and some government agencies even offered payments for certain species. Recreational shooting became common on the mountain, and many birds were killed during migration each year.Photographs showing piles of dead hawks eventually reached conservation campaigner Rosalie Edge in 1933. The images shocked her and convinced her that direct action was needed where official protection had failed.Rather than simply campaigning for stronger wildlife laws, Edge focused on saving the mountain itself. In 1934 she secured roughly 1,400 acres through a lease and appointed experienced bird enthusiasts Maurice and Irma Broun to live and work on the site.Their task was straightforward but demanding. They discouraged hunters, watched over the property and helped establish the area as a refuge instead of a shooting ground. Once the immediate threat had eased, the land was opened to visitors interested in observing migration rather than exploiting it.That decision marked the beginning of Hawk Mountain Sanctuary, recognised as the world's first sanctuary created specifically for birds of prey.Protection of the site quickly led to another lasting contribution. The Brouns began recording every migrating raptor they observed, producing a daily count that started in September 1934.The tradition never stopped. Staff members and volunteers continue the seasonal counts, creating what is regarded as the world's longest continuous record of migrating raptors. The information collected across decades allows scientists to compare annual changes in migration timing, population trends and species abundance.Modern technology has added another layer to this work. Satellite and GPS tracking now reveal where individual birds travel after leaving Hawk Mountain, complementing observations made from the lookout points. Together, the long-running counts and electronic tracking provide a clearer picture of migration routes across North America.Sixteen different species of raptors are regularly recorded at Hawk Mountain. Among the best known are the bald eagle and golden eagle, both large soaring birds that often attract the biggest crowds during migration.Smaller hunters also appear in good numbers. American kestrels, North America's smallest falcons, pass through alongside peregrine falcons, while hawks, vultures and harriers add to the seasonal variety. The exact mix changes through the migration period because different species travel at different times.During spring, from early April to the middle of May, roughly a thousand birds of prey are typically counted. Autumn is far busier. Between the middle of August and the middle of December, seasonal totals average around 18,000 migrating raptors.Migration remains the main reason people travel to Hawk Mountain, with spring and autumn offering the greatest chance of seeing birds overhead. Windy days generally produce the most active flights because stronger air currents help soaring birds continue their journey.The sanctuary has developed facilities for visitors while keeping its conservation purpose intact. South Lookout, one of its principal viewing areas, is wheelchair accessible, allowing more people to experience the migration.Nearly a century after Rosalie Edge acted to stop the annual killing, the same ridge tells a very different story. Instead of marking the end of countless migrations, Hawk Mountain has become a place where birds pass safely overhead and where generations of observations continue to improve understanding of North America's raptors.
Article Summary: Hawk Mountain Sanctuary is the world's first sanctuary created specifically for birds of prey. Visitors can watch bald eagles, broad-winged hawks, peregrine falcons and other species travelling within surprisingly close range. Sixteen different species of raptors are regularly recorded at Hawk Mountain.

Article Title: Powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake hits southern Japan; tsunami warning issued
Article Text: A powerful 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Japan's southern Kyushu region on Tuesday, triggering tsunami warnings, emergency alerts and precautionary evacuations across several prefectures, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).The JMA said the preliminary 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Kumamoto prefecture on Japan's southern main island of Kyushu at a depth of 10 kilometres beneath the seabed.Following the quake, the agency issued "a tsunami warning for a wave measuring 1 metre (3.28 ft)", while Japan's cabinet office issued a tsunami advisory for the Ariake Sea and Yatsushiro Sea.The agency said the tsunami advisory covered Ariake Bay on the western coast of Kumamoto, around 900 kilometres southwest of Tokyo. The US Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said there was no threat of a tsunami beyond local coastlines.Japan's cabinet office disaster management division said the earthquake registered the highest seismic intensity of 7 in the Kumamoto region and urged residents to rely on official information."An earthquake occurred in the Kumamoto region of Kumamoto Prefecture, registering a maximum seismic intensity of 7.Residents in areas where the shaking was strong, in addition to information from the national government and local authorities, please check reliable sources such as television, radio, and the internet, and act calmly," it said.Meanwhile, prime minister Sanae Takaichi said the government had established a task force to monitor the situation and coordinate the response."We are putting people's lives as the top priority," Takaichi said in a message posted on X, urging residents in affected areas to avoid the coastline and remain alert for possible strong aftershocks.The Japanese government activated emergency earthquake warnings for Kumamoto, Nagasaki, Kagoshima, Fukuoka, Saga, Oita and Miyazaki prefectures, all on Kyushu island.According to the National Center for Seismology, the earthquake occurred at 12:57:22 IST with its epicentre at latitude 32.643°N and longitude 130.985°E, at a depth of 70 kilometres.Authorities said electricity supply was disrupted to around 45,600 households in Kumamoto prefecture, according to Kyushu Electric.As a precaution, Shinkansen bullet train services and local train operations across parts of Kyushu were temporarily suspended for safety inspections, while the defence ministry dispatched aircraft to assess the impact.The earthquake revived memories of the devastating Kumamoto earthquakes in 2016, which killed more than 50 people, injured around 1,800 and damaged or destroyed tens of thousands of homes. Restoration work at the historic Kumamoto Castle, which was extensively damaged in the disaster, is expected to continue until 2052.
Article Summary: A 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Japan's southern Kyushu region on Tuesday. The quake triggered tsunami warnings, emergency alerts and precautionary evacuations across several prefectures. The US Pacific Tsunami Warning Center said there was no threat of a tsunami beyond local coastlines.

Article Title: Donald Trump, Zelenskyy discuss Patriot production, Russia peace talks at White House
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump with Ukrainian President Zelenskyy

Patriot production, defence cooperation discussed

Push to restart diplomacy with Russia

Relations between Trump and Zelenskyy improve

Graham's funeral and sanctions push

Ukraine raises Russia-Iran concerns

US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a closed-door meeting at the White House on Tuesday, focusing on expanding Ukraine's defence capabilities, including the production of Patriot missile interceptors, and efforts to revive stalled peace talks with Russia.The meeting in the Oval Office, held ahead of the funeral of late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, came weeks after Trump announced at the Nato summit in Ankara that the US would grant Ukraine a licence to manufacture Patriot air defence systems — a long-standing request from Kyiv.After the talks, Zelenskyy described the meeting as "good" and thanked Trump for the US administration's continued support."The President and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help. We also spoke about diplomacy — it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated," Zelenskyy said in a post on social media.White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt described the meeting as "positive and productive."The discussions centred on strengthening Ukraine's ability to produce advanced defence systems domestically as Russia continues its missile and drone attacks more than four years after invading Ukraine.According to Reuters, Zelenskyy said the two leaders discussed Trump's commitment to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors under licence."We talked with the president about licenses for producing interceptors for the Patriots and other ideas that could help," Zelenskyy said on Telegram.Later in the day, Zelenskyy also met executives from defence giant Lockheed Martin, saying Ukraine and the company were already working on solutions "to move to co-production as quickly as possible".Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, told news agency AP that expanding Patriot interceptor production would benefit not only Ukraine but also the US and its allies as global demand for the systems continues to rise.The leaders also discussed reviving diplomatic efforts to end the war with Russia.According to Reuters, Trump intended to discuss the peace process with Zelenskyy, with a White House official saying, "Now is the time to end the war."Zelenskyy said renewed diplomacy was an important part of the discussions."We also talked about diplomacy – it is important to step up the diplomatic process," he said.US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have agreed to visit Ukraine for the first time as part of efforts to revive mediation with Russia. Zelenskyy had said last week that he had already discussed prospects for renewed peace talks with both officials.The meeting highlighted the improving relationship between Trump and Zelenskyy after a difficult start to Trump's second term.The two leaders had clashed during Zelenskyy's earlier White House visit, but ties have warmed in recent months as Ukraine has sought to strengthen relations with the Trump administration while continuing to resist Russian attacks.Relations have improved as Ukraine has intensified strikes on Russia's oil infrastructure and sought closer defence cooperation with Washington.Zelenskyy's visit coincided with the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's strongest supporters in Washington.After attending the funeral, the Ukrainian president was scheduled to meet US senators on Capitol Hill. Lawmakers are preparing to vote on a bipartisan sanctions package against Russia that Graham had championed before his death.The proposed legislation would impose tariffs on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, and expand sanctions targeting Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior officials, financial institutions and energy projects.Ahead of the meeting, Zelenskyy also alleged that Russia had been assisting Iran by providing satellite imagery of US military bases in the Gulf region, claiming there was a "clear correlation" between those images and subsequent Iranian strikes.Trump, however, downplayed the significance of any such Russian assistance."I don't think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level," Trump told reporters aboard Air Force One on Monday. "And if they have, it has been very un-impactful."The issue comes after Ukraine struck at least one Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea over the weekend, prompting diplomatic exchanges between the foreign ministers of Iran and Ukraine.Ukraine has maintained that its operations are solely aimed at defending itself against Russian aggression and were not intended to target civilian vessels.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a closed-door meeting at the White House on Tuesday. The two leaders discussed expanding Ukraine's defence capabilities, including the production of Patriot missile interceptors. The leaders also discussed reviving diplomatic efforts to end the war with Russia.

Article Title: Donald Trump, Netanyahu hold 'excellent' White House meeting as Iran differences come into focus
Article Text:
File photo: US President Donald Trump with Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu

Differences over Iran surface ahead of talks

Gaza, Lebanon and regional diplomacy on agenda

Domestic pressures and changing political dynamics

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met at the White House on Tuesday for their first face-to-face talks since the two countries launched a joint military campaign against Iran, with both leaders seeking to manage differences over the future course of the conflict.The closed-door meeting lasted nearly 90 minutes and was "positive and productive," White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said, without providing further details, as per AP.After the meeting, Netanyahu described the talks as "excellent", saying they reflected close coordination between the two allies."When I say excellent, I don't mean it in a superficial way," Netanyahu said in a video posted on Instagram."A conversation with full partnership, with mutual support, with an understanding of the common goal of ensuring that Iran does not have nuclear weapons, and other goals as well. One of the best conversations I've had with the President of the United States, our friend Donald Trump."The meeting came against the backdrop of signs of strain in the relationship, particularly over Iran.Ahead of the talks, Trump publicly criticised reports suggesting Netanyahu intended to discuss Israeli intelligence on Iran's alleged activities at Pickaxe Mountain, a site believed to be linked to Tehran's nuclear programme."I know exactly what's going on at Pickaxe," Trump told Fox & Friends.He added that whatever Iran was doing there was "not a big problem" and suggested Netanyahu wanted to keep Washington deeply involved in the issue."Bibi's telling me that because he wants me to stay involved," Trump said."Why do you have to announce to the world?" he added, expressing frustration over the reports.On Monday, Trump acknowledged there were some differences between the two leaders on Iran."We have a little difference," he told reporters. "But pretty close, yeah."According to news agency AP, Netanyahu planned to share Israeli intelligence on Iran's nuclear programme during the visit, while also seeking to understand Trump's strategy towards Tehran in the coming weeks.Speaking before his trip, Netanyahu had said he hoped to hear "what he has in mind" regarding Iran."Because I think, in many ways, it's his decision," Netanyahu told Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures."If he can do so without returning to intense military fighting, that's fine. Why not? But one way or the other, they have to end their nuclear program," he said.Besides Iran, the two leaders were expected to discuss the implementation of the US-Israel framework agreement with Lebanon following the conflict with Hezbollah, as well as efforts to expand the Abraham Accords, according to a White House official cited by AP.Israel has recently agreed to allow the Lebanese Army to deploy in parts of southern Lebanon under a pilot arrangement, with the next round of talks between Israel and Lebanon scheduled to take place in Rome next week, according to the US State Department.On Gaza, Israel's security cabinet has approved a measure that would allow the first members of a proposed international stabilisation force to enter parts of the territory under a US-backed ceasefire framework.The force would initially operate in a limited area in Rafah, although only a few countries have so far pledged troops.The meeting came as both leaders face political challenges at home.Netanyahu is preparing for elections while also dealing with criticism over his handling of relations with the Trump administration.Trump, meanwhile, faces pressure to bring an end to the conflict with Iran amid concerns over its economic impact ahead of November's midterm elections.The relationship between Trump and Netanyahu has fluctuated over the years. While the two leaders initially presented a united front after launching military operations against Iran earlier this year, differences have emerged as Trump has increasingly pursued diplomatic engagement with Tehran while Netanyahu has favoured maintaining military pressure.Israeli political analyst Amit Segal wrote in Israel Hayom that "the Americans are making it clear to the Israelis they are the ones who are running the war," adding that "Israel has been put in the back seat," according to AP.Outside the White House, a small group of demonstrators protested Netanyahu's visit, chanting slogans including "Netanyahu, you're a tyrant" and "Bibi, you're not welcome here," AP reported.The visit also comes at a time when public support for Israel in the United States has declined.An AP-NORC poll published earlier this month found a significant erosion in support for Israel among American adults, while Vice President JD Vance had reportedly warned Israeli officials in June that Trump remained their strongest international ally.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump and Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu met at the White House on Tuesday. It was their first face-to-face talks since the two countries launched a joint military campaign against Iran. Netanyahu described the talks as "excellent", saying they reflected close coordination between the two allies.

Article Title: Gavin Newsom's former aide Ruby Rippey breaks silence on 2007 affair; Kamala Harris advised her to stay silent, California Governor responds through spokesperson
Article Text:
Gavin Newsom's former aide Ruby Rippey breaks silence on 2007 affair; Kamala Harris advised her to stay silent, California Governor responds through spokesperson

Gavin Newsom publicly admitted affair in 2007

Rippey opens up about addiction and guilt

Kamala Harris advised Rippey to stay silent

Rippey rejects being portrayed only as a victim

Gavin Newsom responds through spokesperson

Two decades after a scandal that shook Democratic politics, Ruby Rippey, the former aide who had an affair with California Governor Gavin Newsom, has shared her side of the story for the first time.In a first-person essay published in Vanity Fair, Rippey reflected on the 2007 controversy involving Newsom, who was then the mayor of San Francisco, and the personal and political fallout that followed. Her essay comes as Newsom, 58, is being viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 US presidential race.Rippey, now 54, was working as the secretary to the San Francisco Commission on the Environment when the affair began. At the time, she was married to Alex Tourk, Newsom's close friend and deputy chief of staff.The scandal became public in 2007 when Newsom appeared before reporters at San Francisco City Hall and acknowledged the affair."Everything you’ve heard and read is true," Newsom said at the time.Newsom later addressed the episode in his memoir Young Man in a Hurry, released in February, describing it as the "stupidest and also briefest of affairs."He wrote that he eventually "came clean" to Tourk.However, Rippey challenged that version of events, saying the wording created an impression that Newsom was the one who revealed the truth to Tourk."That detail—subtle but significant—is the one that stays with me," Rippey wrote. "It reads—to me, at least—as a version of events that gives him credit for something I had already done."She added that while the description may be "technically defensible", it suggested that Newsom, rather than her, had taken the step of informing Tourk.In her essay, Rippey said the affair happened during a difficult period in her life, which included struggles with alcoholism and cocaine use.She wrote that the relationship began after a City Hall colleague's wedding in July 2005."We meet and we drink. There is sex, but it isn’t the point. The point is proximity—to power, to being chosen, to feeling newly visible," she wrote.Rippey said she has now been sober for 20 years and that her substance abuse eventually led to a rehabilitation programme in 2006. According to her account, it was during rehab that she wrote a letter to Newsom ending the affair."When I return home from rehab nearly two months later, I try to resume life as a wife and mother," she wrote, adding that Tourk continued working at City Hall without knowing what had happened."For months, I say nothing. The silence settles into my body like a fever. Until one night I am no longer able to carry it," she wrote.Rippey also recalled seeking advice about whether she should publicly address the controversy. She said then-California politician Kamala Harris advised her to wait before making any statement."I tell her people are urging me to speak publicly," Rippey wrote. "She listens, then says simply: 'I wouldn’t say anything right now, Ruby. Just pause. More time will give you better perspective.'"Rippey described Harris' advice as "the best advice" she received during the period.Reflecting on the aftermath of the scandal and the later #MeToo movement, Rippey said she disagreed with narratives that completely removed her responsibility because she was a subordinate.She also recalled being criticised publicly at the time, including by Jennifer Siebel Newsom, Newsom's then-girlfriend and now-wife, who had called Rippey the "culprit" before later apologising.Addressing the broader discussion around power dynamics, Rippey wrote that two realities can exist at the same time."Both things are true: I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly," she wrote.A spokesperson for Gavin Newsom said the governor had already acknowledged his actions and apologised nearly two decades ago."He addressed his role and publicly apologized nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor," spokesperson Izzy Gardon said in a statement.She added that Newsom has since focused on his family and serving Californians and "does not have anything further to add" out of respect for everyone involved.Following the scandal, Alex Tourk left Newsom's reelection campaign and later founded Ground Floor Public Affairs, a firm that has represented companies including Lyft, Amazon and Goodwill.
Article Summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom's former aide Ruby Rippey breaks silence on 2007 affair. Kamala Harris advised her to stay silent, California Governor responds through spokesperson. Newsom is being viewed as a potential contender for the 2028 US presidential race.

Article Title: Why do people claim they crossed over to Canada from the US border by mistake?
Article Text:
Many tourists make the mistake of crossing the border into Canada when visiting Niagara Falls.

Do such mistakes really happen?

A recent Reddit post on a person claiming that a friend, a Palestinian refugee, went inside Canada from the US border and then got detained while coming back has triggered a major debate on such claims. This particular incident goes like this: the Redditor said a friend and the friend's boyfriend wanted to see the US-Canada border in Detroit. They ended up at a spot where they could not turn around and had to cross the border.The guards allowed them to enter and assured them that they would be able to turn back. But border police stopped them when they were entering the US. The boyfriend was a Palestinian refugee with a valid passport and an expired visa. But he had all the paperwork that he filed for the renewal of his visa. The girlfriend was an American citizen and she was released but the boyfriend was detained -- the friend posted on Reddit Many Redditors who claimed to be US citizens commented that it is a pretty common mistake and it happens all the time at several other places too but they faced no problem as they are citizens. But many claimed that if the story was true, the Palestinian with an expired visa would surely be deported. Some asked how people make this mistake while there are clear road signs.The Redditor claimed that it was a mistake and those two friends could have done nothing by the time they realized.The Redditor said the Palestinian man had a residency in Jordan where he could self-deport himself as an option instead of being sent to Palestine."He’s probably on a T passport from Jordan. More than likely won’t be able to return to Jordan and it literally becomes a “What country will take him” situation, outside of Palestine," one user weighed in. "Precedence says the US can hold him up to 6 months(potentially longer, Z vs. Davis case) before putting him in supervised release. He’s likely going to end up going to one of the countries the US has an agreement with. Mexico, El Salvador, Uganda, etc," the advice said.Going by social media responses, such mistakes are possible but only when the travelers are not attentive. The same mistake happens at Niagara Falls too, as it has one American side and one Canadian side. And many tourists inadvertently cross over to the Canadian side.
Article Summary: A recent Reddit post on a person claiming that a friend, a Palestinian refugee, went inside Canada from the US border and then got detained while coming back has triggered a major debate on such claims. Many Redditors who claimed to be US citizens commented that it is a pretty common mistake and it happens all the time at several other places.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Kal Penn: "Growing up, I always had two interests and two passions; one being public service and the other being…" - a reminder that you don't have to fit into one identity
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Kal Penn

"Growing up, I always had two interests and two passions; one being public service and the other being the arts and acting"

The powerful message behind Kal Penn’s quote

The real story behind this quote

Why having more than one passion can actually be a strength

Why nobody needs to fit into just one identity

Why curiosity tends to open doors nobody planned for

Why chasing more than one passion takes real nerve

Why acting and public service actually complement each other

Other famous quotes by Kal Penn

"If you've always grown up seeing people who look like you on screen, I totally understand why a lot of people are like, 'Well, what's the big deal?' But to be invisible, it kind of makes you feel like your possibilities might be limited."

"We're living in a world where people don't have one job or one interest and the idea that these things are mutually exclusive is no longer the way the world works."

"The point of serving your country is not to do your own thing or to go rogue, but to work as part of the process."

"The thing that I enjoy about being an actor and the thing that I enjoy about the arts in general is the ability to make the audience feel an emotion that they weren't intending to feel before they went in."

Why this quote continues to inspire generations

Most people get pushed toward picking one lane early on, one career, one identity, one clear answer to give whenever someone asks what they do. Kal Penn , the actor and former White House official, simply never accepted that framing. "Growing up, I always had two interests and two passions," he said, "one being public service and the other being the arts and acting. " Rather than choosing between the two permanently, he built an unusual career that kept moving back and forth between them, taking each seriously in turn rather than treating one as a hobby and the other as the real job.Penn is directly challenging the idea that a meaningful life needs to be built around a single dream. From an early age, two very different worlds pulled at him, public service, the pull toward contributing to society through government and civic work, and the arts, built around performance and storytelling. Rather than treating those two things as rivals competing for his attention, he found ways to actually pursue both, at different points across his career, instead of settling permanently for just one.This is not just a nice sentiment. Penn actually lived it out in a genuinely dramatic career move.In 2009, while playing Dr. Lawrence Kutner, a regular character on the medical drama House, he left the show entirely to join the Obama administration as Associate Director of the White House Office of Public Engagement. His exit from the show was written into the story as his character's suicide, a jarring way to leave a hit series behind for a government job most actors would never have considered giving up fame for.Born Kalpen Suresh Modi in New Jersey, Penn later wrote a memoir called You Can't Be Serious, describing exactly this pattern of moving between two passions rather than picking one for good. He has also taught at both UCLA and the University of Pennsylvania, adding education into the mix alongside acting and public service.Plenty of people worry that having several genuine interests makes them look unfocused. In practice, mixing different fields together tends to sharpen someone's thinking rather than dilute it. Skills built in one area regularly strengthen performance in another. Communication skills built through acting can make someone a considerably stronger public speaker. Time spent in public service can deepen how an actor actually understands the social issues they end up portraying on screen.People usually get introduced by a single label, teacher, doctor, engineer, actor. In reality, almost nobody is genuinely limited to just one role. A scientist can love music. An engineer can write novels on the side. Penn's own career shows that personal identity can be considerably richer than whatever single job title happens to appear on a business card.Curiosity pushes people past the boundaries they already know well, and trying something genuinely new often opens up opportunities that no amount of careful planning could have predicted in advance. Penn's own willingness to move between acting, government work and teaching let him contribute in several completely different ways rather than committing to just one path for life. Careers today are rarely a straight line anyway, and staying open to unexpected turns tends to make the whole journey more rewarding, not less.Choosing a path that does not look conventional invites doubt from almost everyone around you. Friends and colleagues questioned Penn's decision to leave a hit television show for what looked, from the outside, like a much less glamorous government job. Pursuing more than one genuine passion takes a certain kind of confidence, trusting that different experiences will eventually come together rather than simply pull you apart.Acting and government work look completely different on the surface, one built around storytelling, the other around policy and administration. Underneath that, both genuinely depend on communication, empathy and understanding how people actually think and feel. Penn himself has said that acting lets him make an audience feel something they were not expecting to feel, while public service is really about improving people's lives directly. Different skills, aimed at a similar underlying goal.Careers now shift and combine far more than they used to, with people picking up side projects, changing industries entirely, or blending several genuine interests into one working life. Penn's own path, jumping between acting, government and teaching rather than settling on just one, fits that shift closely. His message is really an invitation to stop treating varied interests as a weakness. They can just as easily become the actual source of a much richer, more interesting life.
Article Summary: Kal Penn is an actor and former White House official. His quote of the day challenges the idea that a meaningful life needs to be built around a single dream. Penn's own career shows that personal identity can be considerably richer than whatever single job title happens to appear on a business card.

Article Title: He ran out of water, but not luck: California man’s mast broke and phone died; after 30 days alone in the Pacific, a container ship found him 900 miles from Hawaii
Article Text:
Photo credit: Hawaii News Now

A voyage gone wrong

Surviving with scraps

Representative image

The rescue at sea

Relief after the ordeal

What happens next

A harsh lesson from the Pacific

A California man has been rescued alive after spending 30 days stranded at sea when his sailboat lost its mast, his phone died and he ran out of gas far from shore. Kai Sato, 39, was found drifting about 900 miles from Hawaii by the crew of a passing container ship, ending a desperate solo voyage that had nearly turned fatal.Sato had left Catalina Island on June 7 hoping to complete his first solo crossing of the Pacific, according to reports from Hawaii News Now and the Seafarers International Union. Instead, he found himself alone in open ocean, badly off course and fighting for survival.What started as an ambitious personal journey quickly unraveled after Sato’s mast snapped and the phone he was using for navigation stopped working. He said he initially tried to motor back toward shore, but the boat ran out of fuel, leaving him “like a sitting duck” as currents pushed him farther south, as per reports.For days, he said, he felt overwhelmed and hopeless. In an interview with Hawaii News Now, Sato said he cried for a week while drifting helplessly and even thought about turning on the motor and suffocating himself. It was a terrifying confession, and a reminder of how quickly isolation at sea can become psychologically unbearable.After several days, however, he forced himself to adapt. He began improvising repairs with whatever he had on board, including PVC pipes and kayak paddles, trying to rig the damaged boat well enough to keep moving.As the days stretched into weeks, Sato’s biggest challenge became water. After about 20 days, he said he had run out of drinking water and had to find another way to stay alive. He used a plastic bag to trap condensation, then drank what he could collect.“I was just licking that to survive,” he said, according to The Guardian.Food was just as uncertain. He survived mainly on oatmeal, along with fish and squid that happened to land on the boat. It was a grim, improvised diet, but enough to keep him going until he reached a shipping lane between California and Hawaii, as per reports.That stretch of ocean proved to be his lifeline.According to the Seafarers International Union, watch standers aboard the M/V George III spotted a small sailboat in distress on July 21. The vessel was approximately 900 miles from Hawaii, and the crew immediately began rescue procedures.The union said the ship’s crew prepared its engines for maneuvering, set up life rings, messenger lines and life-throwing equipment, and then worked to bring Sato safely aboard. They had to make two attempts to lower a rope ladder before the rescue succeeded.Once Sato was pulled close enough, he was able to climb aboard the George III and finally leave his damaged sailboat behind. The union said the rescue took about an hour and a half in total, and that Sato expressed deep gratitude to the crew for saving his life.Sato said the moment he was rescued was overwhelming. Hawaii News Now reported that he described feeling ecstatic and crying from relief after being brought aboard. The crew gave him clothes, fruit and water after his weeks alone at sea, a small but powerful return to normal life after nearly a month of hardship.Images taken during and after the rescue showed just how badly damaged the sailboat was. Its mast had snapped, its sails were left floating below, and the tiny vessel looked no match for the open Pacific that had nearly swallowed it.These detail matters, because it captures the scale of the danger. A broken mast in the middle of the ocean is not just an inconvenience; it can mean the difference between drifting and surviving.Sato is now staying with a relative in Hawaii, but he is already thinking about sailing again. According to Hawaii News Now, he plans to set off for the Philippines in a larger boat.That detail sounds almost unbelievable after what he has just survived, but it also fits the mindset of many long-distance sailors: the ocean can punish mistakes harshly, yet it also keeps drawing people back.For now, though, the story is not about the next voyage. It is about endurance, improvisation and an extraordinary rescue that came just in time.Sato’s ordeal is a stark reminder of how unforgiving the ocean can be when several things go wrong at once. A broken mast, a dead phone, no fuel and no easy access to water would challenge even an experienced crew, let alone someone alone on a small boat.It is also a story about luck and timing. Had the container ship not entered that shipping lane when it did, the outcome might have been very different. Instead, a routine passage across the Pacific became a life-saving encounter.In the end, Sato’s survival came down to stubbornness, improvisation and a rescue that arrived after 30 days too long at sea, but just in time.
Article Summary: Kai Sato, 39, left Catalina Island on June 7 hoping to complete his first solo crossing of the Pacific. His sailboat lost its mast, his phone died and he ran out of gas far from shore. He survived mainly on oatmeal, along with fish and squid that happened to land on the boat. Sato was rescued by the crew of a passing container ship.

Article Title: Florida to carry out two executions on same day, first such move in US in nearly a decade
Article Text:
James Aren Duckett and Dominick Anthony Occhicon (AP Photo)

Two decades-old murder cases

DeSantis expands use of capital punishment

Rare move draws criticism

Oldest inmate in Florida's modern history

Florida is preparing to carry out two executions on Tuesday, becoming the first US state in nearly a decade to execute two inmates on the same day. If both lethal injections go ahead, it will also mark Florida's first same-day executions since 1964 and the first under the modern US death penalty era for the state.According to The New York Post, James Aren Duckett, 68, is scheduled to be executed at noon, followed about six hours later by 80-year-old Dominick Anthony Occhicone at Florida State Prison near Starke.Both inmates had appeals pending before the US Supreme Court at the time of the scheduled executions.Duckett, a former police officer, was sentenced to death for the 1987 rape and murder of an 11-year-old girl. Earlier this year, the Florida Supreme Court temporarily halted his execution to allow DNA testing on decades-old evidence.The tests produced inconclusive results, neither clearing him nor conclusively linking him to the crime, after which the stay was lifted.Occhicone was convicted for the 1986 murders of his former girlfriend's parents. His lawyers argued that his advanced age and medical conditions, including kidney and prostate ailments, could make the execution unconstitutional because of the risk of severe pain. State courts rejected the appeal.The planned executions would be Florida's 11th and 12th this year, continuing a sharp rise in executions under Republican Governor Ron DeSantis.Since early 2025, DeSantis has signed death warrants at a pace unmatched in modern Florida history. The state carried out 19 executions last year, the highest annual total since the death penalty was reinstated nationwide in 1976. Another execution is already scheduled for August.If Tuesday's executions proceed, DeSantis will have overseen 31 executions during his final two years in office, compared with just nine during his first six years as governor.Executing two inmates on the same day is uncommon in the US. The last such instance occurred in 2017, when Arkansas carried out two executions hours apart. Before that, Texas executed two prisoners on the same day in 2000.Death penalty opponents have criticised Florida's decision, arguing that the accelerated pace raises concerns over transparency and the possibility of execution errors. Advocacy groups have urged DeSantis to halt both executions, saying the state is expanding capital punishment despite declining public support.Supporters of the governor's approach argue that long-delayed death sentences should be carried out to provide justice to victims' families. DeSantis has previously said that many of the crimes were committed decades ago and that "justice delayed is justice denied."If executed, Occhicone would become the oldest inmate put to death in Florida's modern history and one of the oldest executed in the US since capital punishment resumed in 1976. His case has renewed debate over executing elderly prisoners who may otherwise die of natural causes while on death row.Florida carries out executions using a three-drug lethal injection protocol consisting of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart.
Article Summary: James Aren Duckett, 68, is scheduled to be executed at noon on Tuesday. Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, will be executed about six hours later. If both lethal injections go ahead, it will be Florida's first same-day executions since 1964 and the first under the modern US death penalty era.

Article Title: 'If you have no criminal record...' US senator wants Green Card for immigrants after 7 years of residency, gets called out as 'traitor'
Article Text:
Senator Alex Padilla was called a traitor after he pushed a new bill to make getting Green Cards easier

What does this Green Card bill say?

The bill proposes to replace a 1972 immigration cutoff with a rolling seven-year residency rule.

The legislation, titled the Renewing Immigration Provisions of the Immigration Act of 1929, would amend Section 249 of the Immigration and Nationality Act, commonly known as the Registry. Currently, the Registry allows the Homeland Security secretary to grant permanent residency to individuals who have lived in the country since a fixed cutoff date of 1 January 1972.

Padilla's bill would replace that static date with a rolling seven-year continuous residency requirement, taking effect 60 days after enactment.

Applicants would need a clean criminal record and must satisfy all existing Green Card eligibility criteria. The bill covers Dreamers, Temporary Protected Status holders, essential workers, and children of long-term visa holders, in addition to skilled workers on employment-based visas.

Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin is co-leading the bill alongside Senator Padilla, with 14 additional senators as co-sponsors.



'Padilla is a traitor'

California senator Alex Padilla reintroduced his 2025 legislation demanding to make Green Card easier for foreign nationals. Those who have stayed in the US continuously for seven years and have no criminal record should get Green Cards, the bill said. But he was called a 'traitor' as he advocated for foreign nationals amid the present anti-immigration wave. "If you’ve built a life here, contributed to this country, and have no criminal record, you should have the chance to stay. It’s been one year since I introduced a bill to do just that," the Democratic leader said."We’ve all witnessed the devastating consequences of Trump and Stephen Miller’s immigration policies — families separated, babies incarcerated, and so many lives lost. It’s why we need a better path forward instead of scapegoating and abusing hardworking immigrants," he said. Congress must act now to pass this simple update to a historically bipartisan provision in the law, he added.While there is zero chance of the bill moving forward, social media users called Padilla a traitor for wanting to make it easier for foreigners to get a Green Card. "Laws are already in place to come here legally. If you didn't, your a criminal. Padilla is a traitor to the constitution & taxpayers," one wrote."Look, that was a horrible bill, that probably why you introduced it while the opposing party was in power. Someone, would just need to enter illegally and avoid getting in trouble for seven years," another wrote.
Article Summary: California senator Alex Padilla reintroduced his 2025 legislation demanding to make Green Card easier for foreign nationals. Padilla's bill would replace a 1972 immigration cutoff with a rolling seven-year residency rule. The bill covers Dreamers, Temporary Protected Status holders, essential workers, and children of long-term visa holders.

Article Title: Trump’s two-front challenge: Shades of 1914 as Zelenskyy and Netanyahu converge on Washington
Article Text:
Netanyahu, Trump, Zelenskyy

TOI correspondent from Washington:

For more than three years, the war in Ukraine and the conflict between Israel and Iran have unfolded as separate geopolitical dramas. On Tuesday however, the two appear closer than ever to becoming chapters of the same story.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Washington around the same time for the funeral of the late Senator Lindsey Graham -- a staunch advocate of both Ukraine's war effort and a hard line against Iran -- with the White House finding itself at the intersection of two conflicts that increasingly overlap.Whether that convergence remains political and contained or turns into something more kinetic and expansive could become one of the defining foreign-policy questions confronting President Trump. Already, some historians and diplomats have begun invoking the pre-1914 period of World War I as an analogy because they see similarities in the way separate regional crises risk becoming interconnected through alliances, miscalculation, and escalation.The immediate trigger is a new confrontation in the Caspian Sea, the world's largest inland body of water, where, according to Zelenskyy, Ukrainian forces carried out long-range strikes against vessels allegedly transporting military cargo between Russia and Iran.Ukraine's Security Service said it targeted ships involved in moving Iranian drones and military supplies, as well as other Russian military assets.Iran rejected that characterization, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing Ukraine of striking an Iranian commercial vessel, killing a sailor, and warning that Kyiv's actions "cannot go unanswered." Tehran summoned Ukraine's charge d'affaires, even as Iranian officials suggested the attack was intended to draw Europe and Nato deeper into Israel vs Iran.Ukraine, for its part, is unapologetic, with the country’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha countering that Iran "has no standing to pretend to be a victim," while arguing that Tehran has been supplying Russia with Shahed drones and other military technology since 2022 – weaponry that he said has killed Ukrainian civilians. Kyiv insists Iran became a participant in the Ukraine war years ago by arming Moscow."Iranians and North Korea have already attacked us," Zelenskyy said in an interview to Sky News, referring to Tehran's drone transfers and North Korea's military assistance to Russia. While maintaining that Kyiv wanted to avoid opening "a new front," he argued that Ukraine had every right to strike military supply chains supporting Russia's war. Western analysts say Russia-Iran military partnership has deepened considerably, and the relationship has increasingly blurred the lines between the European and Middle Eastern theaters.For Zelenskyy, the emerging linkage serves an obvious political purpose. Some analysts argue that Kyiv hopes to convince Washington that helping Ukraine is no longer simply about defending Eastern Europe but also about weakening one pillar of Iran's regional military network. Trita Parsi of the Quincy Institute has suggested that Ukraine may be attempting to merge the two conflicts strategically, making support for Kyiv inseparable from the broader confrontation with Tehran.Remarkably, it is President Trump who has sought to lower the rhetorical temperature. Responding to Zelenskyy's assertion that Russia may have assisted Iranian targeting of US military facilities with satellite intelligence, Trump said on Monday that he intended to discuss the allegation with Russian President Vladimir Putin. "I don't think they've been doing it, certainly not at a high level," he told reporters, adding that if such assistance had occurred, it appeared to have been "very unimpactful. " He is also said to be pushing back against Israeli intelligence feeding Washington about Iranian nuclear assets in Pickaxe mountains, asserting the US has its own intel to make a determination.That measured response reflects Trump's broader diplomatic balancing act. Unlike Senator Graham, whose long career was marked by robust support for military interventions from Iraq to Ukraine and, more recently, Iran, Trump campaigned on avoiding new American wars while simultaneously projecting strength, even as his MAGA supporters say he is being dragged into the wars and he should resist it.Yet critics increasingly question whether his foreign policy reflects a coherent grand strategy or a series of transactional decisions driven by immediate political calculations. His simultaneous efforts to maintain ties with Netanyahu, pursue negotiations with Russia, reassure Nato allies while pressing them to shoulder greater burdens, and cultivate Turkey as a regional partner have created an impression of strategic ambiguity, While his supporters call it flexibility, critics call it improvisation. Trump, meanwhile, must decide for now whether two distant wars can still be managed separately – or whether history has already begun merging them into one.
Article Summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu arrived in Washington around the same time for the funeral of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. The White House finding itself at the intersection of two conflicts that increasingly overlap. Historians have begun invoking the pre-1914 period of World War I as an analogy.

Article Title: New York City flash floods: Heavy rain triggers warnings, hundreds of flights canceled
Article Text:
New York City under flood watch.

Hundreds of flights disrupted

Officials urge residents to stay alert

Storm system follows destructive Midwest weather

New York City and surrounding parts of the Northeast are bracing for heavy rain and possible life-threatening flash flooding, with authorities warning of hazardous travel, flooded roads and major disruptions through Wednesday morning.According to the New York Post, the National Weather Service has placed New York City, Long Island, the Hudson Valley, much of Connecticut, northern New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania under a Flood Watch as slow-moving thunderstorms move across the region.Forecasters say many areas could receive 2 to 5 inches of rain, while isolated downpours may dump 2 to 3 inches in a single hour, significantly increasing the risk of flash flooding.The heaviest rain is expected Tuesday afternoon and evening, with some parts of the Catskills forecast to receive 6 to 8 inches within hours.The US Weather Prediction Center has placed New York City, Long Island and the Mid-Hudson region under a moderate risk of excessive rainfall, while surrounding areas face slight to marginal flood risks.The severe weather has already affected air travel across the New York metropolitan area.Flight disruptions mounted as airlines prepared for the storms, with hundreds of departures canceled at the region's major airports, including John F. Kennedy International Airport, LaGuardia Airport and Newark Liberty International Airport.Officials warned that additional cancellations and delays are possible as the weather system moves through the region.The New York City Emergency Management Department advised residents to allow extra travel time and avoid flooded roads, warning that heavy rain could quickly inundate streets, underpasses and low-lying neighborhoods.Mayor Zohran Mamdani urged residents to prepare for dangerous weather, saying even a short burst of intense rainfall could trigger flash flooding in vulnerable areas.New York Governor Kathy Hochul also urged residents to monitor weather updates and avoid driving through flooded roads."New York State will be experiencing a prolonged rain event beginning Tuesday that will bring heavy rains and cause flash flooding," Hochul said, urging residents to remain vigilant and follow local forecasts. She reiterated the safety message: "When in doubt, turn around, don't drown."The storm system is the same one that swept across the Midwest earlier this week, spawning multiple tornadoes, damaging winds and large hail. It also knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of customers and caused widespread flight disruptions before moving east.Officials noted that New York remains particularly sensitive to heavy rain after the deadly flooding caused by the remnants of Hurricane Ida in 2021, and urged residents to remain cautious as the latest storms move through the region.
Article Summary: New York City, Long Island, the Hudson Valley, much of Connecticut, northern New Jersey and eastern Pennsylvania are under a Flood Watch. Heavy rain is expected Tuesday afternoon and evening, with some parts of the Catskills forecast to receive 6 to 8 inches.

Article Title: In 1998, an Arizona man secretly cut holes through Tucson's street curbs to steal stormwater. The illegal experiment eventually changed city policy
Article Text:
Why Brad Lancaster started cutting curbs without permission

How one illegal project led to real environmental change

How Tucson eventually legalised and expanded water harvesting

Why Tucson's example still matters for other cities

In 1998, a Tucson resident named Brad Lancaster took a saw to the curb outside his home and cut six openings into it, creating small channels to divert rainwater off the street and into the space between the sidewalk and the road. Cutting into a public curb without permission was against city rules, and Lancaster carried out the work quietly, often early on Sunday mornings to avoid drawing attention. City officials remained unaware of what he had done for roughly three years, until Lancaster eventually told them himself, since the results of his experiment had become too striking to keep quiet. What began as one man's unauthorised backyard project would go on to reshape how an entire city thinks about rainwater, eventually leading Tucson to legalise, fund and formally require water harvesting practices across the city. It's a good reminder that policy doesn't always start in a planning meeting. Sometimes it starts with one person, a saw, and a Sunday morning quiet enough that nobody notices until the results are too good to argue with.Tucson sits in the Sonoran Desert and receives only around 11 inches of rainfall a year, making every drop of water a valuable resource in a region long shaped by scarcity. Lancaster, who lived in the Dunbar Spring neighbourhood just north of downtown Tucson, wanted to capture rainwater running off the street and use it to irrigate food-bearing trees and native desert plants along the roadside, rather than letting it disappear into the city's storm drains as wasted runoff.Since existing city rules did not allow residents to alter public street curbs, Lancaster's solution technically broke the law. He proceeded anyway, cutting openings that let stormwater flow directly from the street into planted basins along the sidewalk, allowing mesquite trees, native shrubs and other vegetation to take root and grow using water that would otherwise have simply run off into the sewer system.Over time, the results of Lancaster's curb cuts became difficult to ignore. Trees fed by the diverted rainwater grew into a shaded canopy along his street, and studies of the area later found that soil temperatures in these shaded, water-fed basins ran noticeably cooler than the exposed pavement nearby. According to an account published by the University of Arizona's Water Resources Research Center, the multiple benefits of these small, low-cost interventions eventually became widely recognised among local water officials, including reduced demand for treated drinking water, better water quality, reduced nuisance flooding and the creation of habitat within the city.Neighbours in Dunbar Spring began installing similar curb cut basins of their own, further transforming the character of the streets in the area. What had started as one resident's individual, technically illegal project gradually became a visible, community-wide demonstration of how rainwater could be put to productive use rather than treated purely as a drainage problem to be moved away as quickly as possible.Rather than penalising Lancaster once his curb cuts became known, city officials began working with him to formally legalise the practice. According to city ordinance records , Tucson went on to adopt one of the first ordinances of its kind in the country requiring new commercial developments to meet at least half of their landscaping water needs through harvested rainwater rather than treated municipal supply. The city also began offering rebates to residential homeowners who installed similar streetside water harvesting basins on their own properties.This shift eventually grew into a dedicated municipal programme. According to the City of Tucson's Climate Action Hub , the city's Green Stormwater Infrastructure programme, known as Storm to Shade, was formally approved to install and maintain water harvesting features across public land throughout Tucson, building directly on approaches that had already been developed and tested informally by residents and community groups over the preceding decades.What makes Tucson's story notable is not just the environmental outcome, but the path it took to get there. A change that eventually became official city policy first had to prove itself through years of unauthorised, small scale experimentation, carried out quietly by a private citizen willing to risk breaking a minor city rule in pursuit of a larger environmental goal. City officials have since credited this grassroots groundwork directly, describing municipal programmes today as a formal continuation of work that began below the radar years earlier.As more cities across the arid Southwest grapple with prolonged drought and rising demand for water, Tucson's experience offers a clear example of how small, unofficial interventions can sometimes reshape formal city policy when the results speak clearly enough for themselves. What began as a handful of illegal cuts in a residential curb has since become a documented, institutionalised approach to managing stormwater, one that other water-stressed cities have increasingly looked to as a practical model worth studying.
Article Summary: Tucson resident Brad Lancaster started cutting curbs without permission in 1998. He wanted to divert rainwater off the street and use it to irrigate trees and native desert plants along the roadside. City officials remained unaware of what he had done for roughly three years until Lancaster eventually told them himself.

Article Title: The US buried 85,000 cubic metres of nuclear waste beneath a Pacific island. Now the ocean is rising around it
Article Text:
How Runit Dome was built and what it contains

What the government study found about rising sea levels

Why the dome's location makes it especially vulnerable

What this means for the Marshall Islands going forward

On a remote island in the Marshall Islands, a concrete dome built more than four decades ago holds roughly 85,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste left over from the United States' Cold War-era nuclear testing programme. Known officially as Runit Dome and locally as The Tomb, the structure was built between 1977 and 1980 to seal off contaminated soil and debris from 43 nuclear weapons tests carried out by the US military across Enewetak Atoll between 1948 and 1958. The dome's concrete cap sits directly above a blast crater that was never lined underneath, and rising sea levels are now pushing seawater further into contact with the waste inside, prompting the US Congress to order a formal government study into the risks the site poses as the climate continues to change. What makes Runit Dome such an unsettling case study is the mismatch in timescales, a Cold War fix built for a world that assumed stable coastlines, now facing conditions its 1980 engineers had no real way of predicting.Runit Dome sits on Runit Island, part of Enewetak Atoll, inside a crater created by an 18 kiloton nuclear test known as Cactus, carried out in 1958. Following the end of nuclear testing in the region, around 4,000 US servicemen worked between 1977 and 1980 to gather contaminated soil, military equipment and other radioactive debris scattered across the atoll and bury it inside this crater, which was then capped with an 18-inch-thick layer of concrete.Because the underlying crater was never lined at the bottom, the waste sits in direct contact with the surrounding porous coral and groundwater, which US officials at the time considered an acceptable risk given the site's remote location.According to acongressional report published by the US Department of Energy , Congress directed the department in 2021 to study the impacts of climate change on the Runit Dome site, along with other environmental hazards resulting from the broader nuclear testing programme carried out across the Marshall Islands. The Department of Energy contracted the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory to lead this assessment, bringing together climate scientists, ocean modellers, environmental scientists and health physicists to study the site in detail.The resulting study modelled how rising sea levels and storm surges could affect the site both under current conditions and in projected conditions for the year 2090, including a scenario involving a hypothetical structural failure of the dome itself. According to the same Department of Energy report, researchers found that storm surge combined with gradual sea level rise would have the greatest influence on how radioactive material might move and spread across the atoll over time, more so than the dome's physical integrity alone.Despite these concerns, the study's overall findings offered some reassurance regarding immediate risk to nearby residents. The report concluded that current and projected future conditions, including a hypothetical dome failure, did not indicate an increased health risk to residents of inhabited islands within Enewetak Atoll, and that any changes in radiological exposure to marine life within the lagoon were not expected to meaningfully affect the health or diversity of the atoll's ecosystem.Much of Runit Island sits only a few metres above sea level, leaving very little buffer between the structure and rising tides. Since the dome was completed in 1980, sea levels in the surrounding region have already risen measurably, and climate projections suggest this trend will continue well into the coming decades, gradually increasing the frequency and intensity of storm surges capable of reaching the site.The Department of Energy's assessment specifically identified this combination of gradual sea level rise and episodic storm surges, rather than a single catastrophic collapse, as the primary long-term concern for the site. This distinction matters for how the risk is understood, since it points toward slow, cumulative environmental change as the main driver of potential future exposure, rather than a sudden structural failure of the dome itself.The Runit Dome remains a deeply sensitive issue for the Marshall Islands, a nation whose communities were displaced and exposed to fallout during decades of US nuclear testing before the cleanup effort that created the dome even began. Even as the Department of Energy's study found no immediate elevated health risk under current or modelled future conditions, the underlying reality remains that a large volume of radioactive material sits in an unlined crater on a low-lying island in a region facing among the most severe sea level rise projections in the world.As climate change continues to reshape coastlines across the Pacific, Runit Dome stands as a stark example of how decisions made decades ago, under very different environmental assumptions, are now being reassessed under conditions their original designers never fully anticipated. The Department of Energy's ongoing monitoring and periodic climate impact assessments suggest that Runit Dome will likely remain the subject of continued scientific and political attention for years to come, particularly as sea level projections for the region continue to be refined.
Article Summary: Runit Dome holds 85,000 cubic metres of radioactive waste left over from the United States' Cold War-era nuclear testing programme. The structure was built between 1977 and 1980 to seal off contaminated soil and debris from 43 nuclear weapons tests carried out by the US military across Enewetak Atoll between 1948 and 1958. The dome's concrete cap sits directly above a blast crater that was never lined underneath. Rising sea levels are now pushing seawater further into contact with the waste inside.

Article Title: One killed as violence, rigging claims rock first phase of PoJK polls
Article Text:
PPP alleged that 35-year-old party worker Mukhtar Younus was shot dead. (File photo)

Poll Vote & Share your view What is most important to you during elections? Peaceful voting Fair voting 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The first phase of elections in Pakistan-occupied Jammu & Kashmir (PoJK) was marred by violence on Monday, with rival political parties accusing each other of electoral malpractice after a political worker was killed and several others were injured during polling conducted in illegally occupied Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir.However, eyewitnesses claimed that at least 14 people were killed in police firing in Rawalakot last evening. Imtiaz Aslam, core member, Joint Awami Action Committee, said: "Pakistan terrorist forces fired upon our innocent youth today; as a result, 14 of our young men were killed. I make an earnest appeal to overseas Kashmiris: you must stage protests outside Pakistani embassies, human rights organisations worldwide, and the UN. "The Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) alleged that 35-year-old party worker Mukhtar Younus was shot dead during voting in Nikyal in Kotli district. The party blamed supporters of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) for the firing."Our party worker, Mukhtar Yunus, was killed and two others injured during incidents of firing by the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) candidates," the PPP said. PPP chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari questioned the role of the authorities after the incident."Where are the relevant authorities? What is the Election Commission doing?" he asked.The killing intensified an already bitter contest, with the PPP and PML-N accusing each other of rigging and intimidation in several constituencies. According to local media reports, confrontations between rival supporters briefly disrupted polling at a number of booths.The Express Tribune reported that Sindh local government minister Saeed Ghani accused the PML-N of orchestrating the violence. He claimed the party had received information suggesting the firing was carried out by the PML-N candidate or his supporters and alleged that several PPP workers were also injured.More than 1.4 million voters were eligible to vote in the opening phase, which covered 13 Assembly constituencies across Bhimber, Mirpur and Kotli. Around 300 candidates are in the fray. Polling for the so-called legislative assembly is being conducted in three phases until August 10.The assembly has 53 seats, of which 45 are directly elected. The remaining eight are reserved for women, technocrats and clerics.Former prime minister Imran Khan 's Pakistan Tehreek-i-Insaf (PTI) stayed away from the elections, while the Joint Awami Action Committee remains banned following last month's unrest.The committee had spearheaded weeks of protests demanding the abolition of 12 refugee seats in the assembly. The demonstrations, which lasted for nearly 50 days, turned violent after the government rejected the demand. According to PTI, more than 100 people were killed during the unrest. The authorities subsequently outlawed the committee.India has described the protests as the result of Islamabad's long-standing exploitation and administrative oppression in the territory under its forcible occupation. New Delhi has also criticised reports of police action against protesters.Meanwhile, an official alleged that the electoral exercise was largely symbolic, claiming the Pakistan military had already determined the outcome.The official further alleged that the military, led by field marshal Asim Munir, intended to tighten its grip over the political landscape in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and prevent any future protest movement from gaining momentum.
Article Summary: Pakistan Peoples Party (PPP) alleged that 35-year-old party worker Mukhtar Younus was shot dead during voting in Nikyal in Kotli district. The party blamed supporters of the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (PML-N) for the firing.

Article Title: PoK protests: Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts
Article Text:
Thousands march to Muzaffarabad after failed talks; polls delayed in two districts

Talks collapse, protesters hit the streets

Elections overshadowed by unrest

Protests in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) intensified on Monday as thousands of demonstrators began marching towards Muzaffarabad after negotiations between the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) and the authorities broke down, while election officials postponed legislative assembly polls in two districts amid the unrest.The Election Commission deferred voting in the Sudhnoti and Rawalakot constituencies until August 10, citing an ongoing sit-in led by the Public Action Committee (PAC).The postponement comes as a weeks-long protest movement continues to disrupt public life and cast uncertainty over the electoral process.The latest escalation followed the collapse of talks between JAAC leaders and the government on Saturday. Protest organisers alleged that authorities refused to release detained activists, withdraw criminal cases against protesters or agree to the committee's core demands.After the negotiations failed, JAAC issued an ultimatum, asking the government to formally notify acceptance of its demands by 1pm on July 27. It warned that if no action was taken, thousands of supporters would march from Rawalakot to Muzaffarabad — a call that was subsequently carried out.The demonstrations mark the latest phase of a protest campaign that has entered its 52nd day.The political crisis unfolded alongside the first phase of polling in 13 constituencies of the Mirpur division. However, political parties said the prolonged demonstrations had severely affected electioneering across the region.Campaign rallies, public meetings and door-to-door outreach have reportedly been disrupted by strikes and sit-ins, while candidates have expressed uncertainty over voter participation if the protests continue.Residents told local media that public interest in the elections had sharply declined, with many believing that longstanding grievances and basic rights should be addressed before any electoral exercise.
